<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Composite indexes for access patterns

## Scenario

A support queue lists recent open tickets per tenant. A generic status-only index remains slow for busy tenants.

## Failure modes

Column order may prevent useful ordering. Too many indexes slow writes and increase disk and maintenance costs. A small test table can hide poor plans.

## Explain it simply

Arrange the index in the order that matches how most queries narrow and sort the data.

## Implementation guidance

For WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = 'open' ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC, a starting candidate is an index beginning with the equality columns followed by the sorted columns. Verify with actual plans and data distributions across tenants, including rows with equal timestamps. Validate the exact query shape and compare index size, write cost and lookup latency before removing old indexes.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Equality filters and a bounded ordered read dominate** Use a composite index aligned with equality keys and the ordered range, validating with plans. Index maintenance adds write and storage cost.
- **Multiple independent query shapes have different cardinalities** Choose indexes from measured workload and validate each representative plan. Specialization can make maintenance harder and redundant indexes should be removed.

## Verification

- Compare EXPLAIN estimates with realistic data and verify examined rows.
- Measure write overhead and test ordering for equal sort values.

# End-to-end data retention and deletion

## Scenario

A workspace administrator removes a project. Search, caches, background queues and backups may still contain associated data.

## Failure modes

Removing one row can leave replicas, exports or search entries. Immediate backup rewriting can conflict with recovery procedures and legal holds.

## Explain it simply

List the places that keep a copy, remove the live copies and document when recoverable backups age out.

## Implementation guidance

Assign deletion a stable request ID and inventory the authoritative rows, versions, derived views, queue payloads and export destinations touched by it. Record progress or the allowed expiration window per destination. When restoring snapshots, reapply deletions still required before opening access to restored data. Use a synthetic customer record to prove direct lookups, search and restored views all follow the policy, including the explicit exception for a legal hold.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Operational copies must stop serving deleted records** Record the deletion durably, apply it to projections and verify acknowledgements or convergence. Propagation takes time and failures require a clear reconciliation path.
- **Backup copies rotate under an approved retention policy** Scope access, age out snapshots and replay applicable deletions after restoration. Recovery remains possible only within documented retention bounds.

## Verification

- Trace a seeded record through each store and confirm authorized deletion propagates.
- Restore a backup and verify previously deleted records do not reappear in production views.

## Sources

- [Amazon S3 lifecycle expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-expire-general-considerations.html)

# Exact money values and rounding boundaries

## Scenario

An invoicing service splits a discount across seats, applies tax and must preserve the total users see on the invoice.

## Failure modes

Currency scales differ. Independent per-line rounding can lose cents, and integer types encounter overflow when aggregated without a limit.

## Explain it simply

Use an exact representation and decide where rounding happens so line items still add to the displayed total.

## Implementation guidance

Represent amounts together with currency and choose the currency-specific unit at system boundaries. In a same-currency 100-cent allocation across three identical lines, one reproducible rule yields 34, 33 and 33 cents by assigning the leftover cent under a stable line order. Define when tax and discount round, and use checked addition and multiplication. Test fractional discounts, signed refunds, unsupported currency scales and totals near the storage limit.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Currency uses well-defined minor units and rates are separate** Store integer minor units with the currency and choose checked arithmetic for totals. Conversions and percentage calculations still need a rounding policy.
- **Calculations require fractional accounting precision** Use a decimal type with explicit scale and rounding at the agreed boundary. Database and application serialization must preserve the same representation.

## Verification

- Assert that split amounts reconcile to the original total across rounding ties.
- Test zero- and three-decimal currencies, negative refunds and configured bounds.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# SQLite or a database server

## Scenario

A local note tool opens a single workspace file. A later team edition would support many remote editors and centralized backups.

## Failure modes

Sharing an embedded database over unsupported network filesystems can corrupt assumptions. A database server adds operational cost to simple local tooling.

## Explain it simply

Use a local database when the data belongs to one runtime and move to a server when many remote writers need coordination.

## Implementation guidance

List cooperating processes, host locations and who owns backups before choosing the file format. For one workstation, an embedded database can give migrations and transactions with minimal operations. Back it up with its supported mechanism. When remote clients need shared writers or centralized access, a service-managed database moves that coordination to a defined owner. Test abrupt shutdown recovery and verify that a restore can be opened with the expected schema.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A process owns a local file with modest write concurrency** Use an embedded database and document file ownership, backups and transaction boundaries. Write contention and cross-host access still require care.
- **Independent hosts routinely write shared state** Use a database server with controlled access, concurrency and restore procedures. Deployment and operational complexity increase.

## Verification

- Exercise realistic concurrency and recovery on the intended filesystem.
- Restore a representative backup and verify read/write access and migrations.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Search index freshness and recoverability

## Scenario

A job board updates postings in its primary store and asynchronously indexes them for keyword search.

## Failure modes

Lost events leave records stale. Rebuilding in-place can show partial results, and opening access before deletion events finish can expose removed entries.

## Explain it simply

Keep the main record authoritative and make it possible to rebuild search without losing or exposing entries.

## Implementation guidance

Give every indexed change a stable document ID and source version, including deletes. Build replacement indexes from a snapshot and replay changes after that snapshot until caught up before an atomic read-alias switch. Guard sensitive reads against authoritative access when staleness is unacceptable. Measure source-to-query lag by operation type and verify that a late old update cannot resurrect a record deleted just before cutover.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Low lag is acceptable and changes can be replayed** Publish durable versioned changes, apply idempotently and rebuild into a versioned index before switching. Additional lag, monitoring and storage are expected.
- **Strong freshness is required for a subset of records** Confirm critical membership or access against the source and use an appropriate exact lookup. Authoritative checks add latency, particularly after a broad search.

## Verification

- Drop and replay changes and verify the rebuilt index equals the expected projection.
- Switch indexes under writes and confirm deletions and authorization are preserved.

## Sources

- [Elastic index aliases](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/aliases.html)
- [AWS transactional outbox pattern](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Inverted index for text search

## Scenario

A policy archive has thousands of documents. A query should find records containing both words without reading all document bodies.

## Failure modes

Singular/plural normalization changes meaning in some domains. Newly updated records can lag the primary store, and query syntax must be compiled safely.

## Explain it simply

Store a list of document IDs for each word so a search can combine just the lists it needs.

## Implementation guidance

Specify how the analyzer handles case, accents, stop words and product codes before exposing search. For AND matching, tokenize the query and intersect the postings for its terms. Keep syntax generated by the application separate from user text. Store a reference to authoritative records rather than treating search results as permissions. Test inflections, punctuation-heavy codes and authorization changes alongside recall and response time as the corpus grows.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **General term search needs ranking and tokenization** Use a text index with documented analyzers, postings intersections and scoring. Index size and update lag must be monitored.
- **Only exact small identifier lookups are required** Use a keyed index or simple prefix lookup matching the stated contract. This preserves exact semantics but provides no relevance ranking.

## Verification

- Test phrase, spelling and multi-term fixtures with known correct results.
- Update and delete source records, then verify search freshness and rebuild semantics.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# LRU cache eviction and admission

## Scenario

A local thumbnail decoder has a fixed memory budget. Recently viewed items are likely to be reopened, but a large scan can displace them.

## Failure modes

Entry count ignores object size and scans can evict the working set. Mutating the recency list and lookup table separately risks inconsistency.

## Explain it simply

When the cache fills up, remove the item that has gone unused longest if recent use predicts what comes next.

## Implementation guidance

Combine lookup and recency updates behind one synchronization boundary. If thumbnails vary greatly, account in decoded bytes and define what happens when a single item exceeds the cache budget. Update weight for replacement and remove entries until the total fits. Replay a hot working set followed by a one-off scan to compare hit rate and memory against a frequency or admission policy.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Recent use predicts reuse and bounds are simple** Use a bounded LRU with reliable recency updates and track bytes where entries vary in size. A one-time scan can still evict frequently used entries.
- **Repeated frequency matters more than short-term recency** Compare LFU or admission policies against replayed access traces. Additional state and aging logic increase implementation cost.

## Verification

- Test hits, evictions, updates to existing keys and the exact capacity boundary.
- Replay a scan-heavy trace and report hit rate and bytes alongside runtime.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Object retention and deletion lifecycle

## Scenario

A company allows trash recovery for a week and must delete expired objects while retaining legal holds when they apply.

## Failure modes

Deleting a current key can leave earlier versions recoverable. Expiration rules may be asynchronous and retention policies may override cleanup.

## Explain it simply

Define how long copies stay recoverable and verify which copies actually disappear at the end of that period.

## Implementation guidance

Design separate policies for the current object, earlier versions, delete markers and incomplete multipart uploads. Keep a way to verify that a marked deletion actually converges to storage expiry within the allowed window. Model restore and legal hold explicitly, including which actor can release a regulation-driven hold. Prove with a versioned test object that a delete marker hides the current name while older version retention follows policy.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Normal recovery and cost control dominate** Use versioned buckets with explicit current, noncurrent and incomplete-upload lifecycle rules. Lifecycle changes are asynchronous and need monitoring.
- **Some objects must remain immutable for a stated period** Use appropriate retention locks or holds and audit authorized transitions separately. Irreversibility and storage cost need deliberate ownership.

## Verification

- Verify expected state for current and noncurrent versions after logical deletion.
- Test restore and expiry with representative lifecycle settings and hold states.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Replica lag and read-your-writes

## Scenario

A customer changes their shipping address and refreshes immediately. Analytics queries can tolerate lag, but the checkout preview cannot.

## Failure modes

A fixed time window is weaker than tracking a commit position when lag exceeds the estimate. Session-only state can diverge across devices.

## Explain it simply

After you save a change, send your next reads somewhere that has already seen that change.

## Implementation guidance

Choose a consistency path per user operation. After an address change, route the follow-up checkout read to the primary or use a commit position token and serve only replicas that have replayed it, with bounded wait and primary fallback. Decide how another device retrieves an updated position or uses a source read. With an artificially lagging replica, prove that the preview reflects the new address while analytics can remain within its allowed staleness.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A subset of reads needs guaranteed freshness** Read from the primary or a replica known to have reached the write position. Primary load or waiting time increases only for gated reads.
- **Stale reads are acceptable with a clear product contract** Read replicas with a staleness budget and monitor lag, falling back when it exceeds policy. Users may briefly see an older value.

## Verification

- Pause replay and assert critical read-after-write returns the committed value.
- Test cross-device reads, failover and fallback under extended lag.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Transaction isolation for cross-row invariants

## Scenario

An on-call roster can release a person only if at least one other person remains on duty. Two operators make independent changes simultaneously.

## Failure modes

Two transactions may read the same safe amount and update different rows under snapshot isolation. Retrying the final statement alone can retain stale assumptions.

## Explain it simply

Make the database reject one of two changes if accepting them together would violate the rule.

## Implementation guidance

Define the invariant across all rows that matter. If each operator independently updates a different roster row, checking the remaining count first can allow both changes. Guard a shared row or use a fully serializable transaction and retry it from its first read on a serialization conflict. Keep retries bounded and postpone irreversible external actions until the commit outcome is known. Test two transactions that read before either attempts a write.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A clear row or unique constraint represents the invariant** Use a constraint or a short transaction with the specific guarded row. Hot coordination rows can cause contention.
- **The invariant spans rows without a stable lock key** Use serializable isolation and retry the full transaction on serialization failure. Aborts become expected and hooks must not duplicate external effects.

## Verification

- Reproduce write skew with two connections and verify the invariant stays true.
- Exercise transaction retry after a serialization abort and check effect boundaries.

## Sources

- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
- [PostgreSQL constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Expand-and-contract schema changes

## Scenario

An order system splits a free-text address into columns. Older workers need time to deploy and existing records must be transformed in batches.

## Failure modes

A table rewrite can hold locks. A backfill can overwrite recent app writes, and destructive cleanup invalidates rollback assumptions.

## Explain it simply

Add the replacement shape, move and verify existing data, switch traffic, then retire the old shape.

## Implementation guidance

Expand with a compatible field, deploy writers that preserve both representations as needed, then backfill in small restartable batches. Guard each backfill write against changes since the row was read. Compare old and new representations before switching reads, and remove the old field only after the rollback window and old consumers are gone. Rehearse aborting late in the rollout while an older worker is still running.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Persistent data must remain live across a mixed rollout** Add compatible fields, deploy compatible readers and writers, backfill in restartable batches and verify before contract. Temporary complexity buys a reversible migration phase.
- **The table is small and downtime is explicitly acceptable** Use a short planned maintenance migration with a tested snapshot and rollback. Users need clear outage expectations and operational timing.

## Verification

- Trigger concurrent writes during a resumed backfill and verify newer values survive.
- Run read and write paths for old data and new data before destructive cleanup.

# Keyboard navigation and focus management

## Scenario

A document viewer opens a confirmation dialog from a row's action button. Keyboard users must be able to complete it and continue from the right row.

## Failure modes

Hidden or removed elements can retain focus. Custom widget keys may conflict with text entry, and focus can be lost when a list refreshes.

## Explain it simply

Let people reach every action from the keyboard and return them to the place they were working.

## Implementation guidance

Use a real button to open the dialog, choose a meaningful initial focus target, and keep modal keyboard focus in the dialog until it closes. Restore focus to the triggering row control or a logical replacement if that row is gone. Test the full sequence with Tab, Shift+Tab and Escape where supported, as well as another interaction following a refreshed list. Keyboard behavior and an accessibility tree inspection complement automated checks.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Native HTML elements match the intended behavior** Use semantic controls and manage focus only at clear transitions. Native defaults reduce complexity but design and browser behavior need testing.
- **A composite or modal widget needs custom focus behavior** Follow the relevant ARIA authoring pattern and test actual interaction with keyboard and assistive technology. Custom keyboard handling introduces more states and maintenance.

## Verification

- Open, navigate, dismiss and reopen using only a keyboard.
- Verify focus after deleting the invoking row or replacing a focused control.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Rendering priority and loading strategy

## Scenario

A product catalog loads a large gallery and analytics before rendering the main title and hero content.

## Failure modes

Lazy-loading the largest above-the-fold image can delay it. Preloading too much competes for bandwidth and a lab run can miss slow device behavior.

## Explain it simply

Load the content people need first, then fill in the rest as bandwidth and rendering time allow.

## Implementation guidance

Identify the actual largest content element on cold, throttled navigations. Keep its resource discoverable early and avoid deferring it solely because images elsewhere are lazy-loaded. Defer nonessential modules and size visible assets before they arrive to limit layout shifts. Compare field or representative lab measurements for both initial paint and interaction, and remeasure if an optimization changes which element is largest.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A small above-the-fold artifact determines perceived load time** Prioritize critical content and measure navigations under realistic cache, CPU and network conditions. Priority hints must remain selective and responsive to changes.
- **Large media is below the initial viewport** Defer offscreen assets with known sizes and test scrolling and slow networks. Content arrives later and should not jump the layout.

## Verification

- Measure render timing and layout shifts before and after the change.
- Verify the critical content is not deferred and remains usable without optional analytics.

# Form validation and error feedback

## Scenario

A membership form checks required details locally while the server enforces account uniqueness and allowed transitions.

## Failure modes

Client validation can be bypassed. Server errors attached in the wrong order can confuse screen reader and keyboard users.

## Explain it simply

Let the page catch easy mistakes quickly while the server checks the rules that determine whether a submission can succeed.

## Implementation guidance

Use the client to show immediate, accessible field feedback but enforce uniqueness, permissions and allowed state transitions at the server boundary. Map stable server error codes back to their field or form and preserve input on recoverable failures. On a duplicate registration race, require one successful account and an understandable error from the other submission. Exercise both the native keyboard path and a submission without enhancement.

- **Input mistakes are local and cheaply detectable** Use native constraints or client checks and surface field-level messages with accessible links. Client feedback is a convenience and must agree with server semantics.
- **The rule depends on current stored data** Validate atomically on the server and return a stable error code tied to the relevant field or form. Clients must keep entered values, handle outdated state and present the error in context.

## Verification

- Submit invalid and race-prone input directly to the server endpoint.
- Verify users can discover errors, fix them and retain unrelated field values.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Optimistic UI and reconciliation

## Scenario

A user toggles a bookmark quickly on and off while a slow request is still pending.

## Failure modes

Restoring a snapshot from the first failed request can overwrite a newer action. Optimistically confirming irreversible or uncertain operations can mislead users.

## Explain it simply

Show the likely update right away for safe actions, then reconcile it with the confirmed result in the right order.

## Implementation guidance

Attach a mutation identity or revision to each optimistic action and merge acknowledgements against the latest requested state. If the first bookmark action fails after a later toggle succeeds, remove only its projection and leave the later action intact. Keep irreversible or externally pending operations visible as pending until confirmed. Test arrival orders of both successes and errors, plus authoritative refetch after disconnect.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The action is reversible and succeeds most of the time** Use a scoped optimistic patch with a mutation version, pending state and reconciliation. Failure and later mutations need explicit recovery semantics.
- **The action is irreversible or failure is costly** Show pending status until the server confirms the effect. Feedback feels slower but the displayed outcome remains trustworthy.

## Verification

- Resolve repeated mutations in reverse order and assert the last intent wins when accepted.
- Force a failed mutation and verify accessible recovery without corrupting newer state.

## Sources

# Progressive enhancement for essential actions

## Scenario

An appointment portal relies on a large bundle before a form can submit. Some visitors arrive with scripts blocked or delayed.

## Failure modes

Duplicating validation across enhanced and ordinary submissions can create incompatible semantics. Browser navigation and field retention can diverge.

## Explain it simply

Make the basic form work first, then improve it when scripting and network conditions allow.

## Implementation guidance

Build an ordinary form action, server validation and a result or redirect that works without a client application. Enhance the same contract to update inline and announce pending, error and success states. Preserve user-entered data on recoverable validation errors. Run the core flow with scripting disabled, then repeat on a slow connection where the server response completes before hydration.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A workflow can be expressed using native navigation or forms** Provide a server-backed baseline and enhance the same endpoint with compatible client behavior. Some rich interactions need alternative, simpler flows.
- **The interaction genuinely requires client-side state** Provide an accessible status, error recovery and a clear fallback for unsupported contexts. A richer client raises the minimum runtime floor.

## Verification

- Complete the essential flow without optional scripts.
- Compare validation and duplicate submission behavior under slow and normal loads.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Cancelling stale frontend requests

## Scenario

An operator types a search query and the earlier slow response arrives after the newer query's results.

## Failure modes

Cancellation is best effort and a response can resolve just before abort. Loading indicators may be cleared by a superseded request.

## Explain it simply

Ignore results that belong to an old query and cancel unnecessary work when the browser can.

## Implementation guidance

Keep a sequence number for the active request or scope cached results to an immutable query key containing the inputs that affect the response. Pass the cancellation signal to the network operation and compare identity before applying a result, error, or loading completion. Simulate selecting A, selecting B, and receiving A last despite abort. Verify that B keeps both its visible results and loading/error ownership.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A new request supersedes the previous display state** Cancel earlier fetches when possible and gate applied results by current request identity. The server may keep working after the browser cancels.
- **Requests populate independent cached keys** Preserve their separate results and show data scoped to the currently selected key. The cache needs size, retention and invalidation rules.

## Verification

- Resolve two responses in reverse order and verify the screen matches current input.
- Unmount or abort a request and verify errors and loading state remain consistent.

## Sources

- [WHATWG Fetch standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/)
- [TanStack Query cancellation](https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/query-cancellation)

# Responsive tables and usable data views

## Scenario

An operations dashboard compares names, statuses and twelve readings per row on a mobile phone.

## Failure modes

Turning cells into arbitrary cards can remove header associations. Hiding columns by default may hide data required for a decision.

## Explain it simply

Keep the relationships between values and headings clear even when only part of the table fits on the screen.

## Implementation guidance

Retain semantic column and row headers for the comparison table. Let the table scroll in its own region when comparing requires both dimensions, so surrounding content can still reflow. Name the region where appropriate and preserve access to all columns by keyboard and touch. For a detail layout, repeat each field label alongside its value and keep a way back to the originating row. Test long localized headers, zoom, frozen columns and a narrow viewport with a user trying to compare two readings.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Comparing columns is the main task** Keep semantic table markup with labeled horizontal scrolling and sticky headers where appropriate. A small viewport still limits simultaneous context.
- **Reviewing one record is the main mobile task** Offer a compact detail view with clear labels and a route back to the table. Maintaining two layouts requires shared data and behavior.

## Verification

- Test ties between headers and cells with a screen reader.
- Verify all required information is reachable at narrow width and high zoom.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Location minimization and aggregation

## Scenario

A neighborhood activity view needs aggregate hotspots but has no reason to store exact trip traces indefinitely.

## Failure modes

Precise tracks can identify people even without names. Sparse aggregates can expose individual routes and access settings can be broader than intended.

## Explain it simply

Collect only the location detail the feature needs and avoid publishing tiny groups that can identify someone.

## Implementation guidance

Start with the aggregate decision the activity view needs and choose a bin width, time bucket and minimum cohort size that fit it. Suppress sparse buckets and review combinations of outputs that could isolate one trip. If exact coordinates are used during ingestion, restrict access and keep a separate short retention rule. Test a bucket with one participant and successive overlapping windows, not just a well-populated district.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Aggregate spatial patterns meet product requirements** Coarsen at collection or aggregation time, use retention bounds and avoid releasing sparse groups. Precision decreases, and coarsening is not a proof of anonymity.
- **A specific user-facing action needs precise location briefly** Use narrowly scoped consent and processing, minimize storage, and document deletion behavior. The feature must work or degrade gracefully when users decline.

## Verification

- Exercise accepted and declined location permissions and verify data collection scope.
- Verify sensitive raw samples and sparse aggregates are not exported through public paths.

## Sources

- [W3C Geolocation specification](https://www.w3.org/TR/geolocation/)
- [NIST Privacy Framework](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework)

# Coordinate systems and distance correctness

## Scenario

A delivery app compares radius eligibility in kilometers across shops near the equator and far north.

## Failure modes

Euclidean distance on longitude and latitude degrees gives different scales by latitude. Axis order and crossing the date line can invalidate fixtures.

## Explain it simply

Store what the coordinates mean and calculate distance in a unit that is consistent across regions.

## Implementation guidance

Record the coordinate reference system and distance unit at the API boundary. GeoJSON positions are longitude then latitude, while planar distance requires a projection suited to the region. A nationwide or date-line-spanning radius query needs geography-aware handling. Use fixtures that deliberately swap axes, straddle the date line, and place close points at very different latitudes.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Data spans broad geographic regions** Use geography-aware distance or a geodesic calculation with explicit axis order and units. Some operations are more expensive and projections still matter for display.
- **Data is limited to a known local area** Use an appropriate projected coordinate system for planar analysis. Results depend on the projection's region and distortion characteristics.

## Verification

- Verify distances with known reference points at multiple latitudes.
- Cover longitude wrap and reject swapped or out-of-range coordinates.

## Sources

- [PostGIS ST_DWithin](https://postgis.net/docs/ST_DWithin.html)

# Traffic estimation from location samples

## Scenario

A fleet operator wants alerts on sudden slowdown across delivery routes using only consenting fleet vehicle observations.

## Failure modes

Stationary phones and groups in the same vehicle bias aggregates. Sparse windows, GPS errors and route mis-matching produce false alerts.

## Explain it simply

Compare recent vehicle speeds with normal speeds for that road and show uncertainty when observations are sparse.

## Implementation guidance

Attach uncertainty to each map-matched observation and aggregate only sufficiently supported windows for a defined road segment and direction. Exclude stationary or duplicate samples using documented rules and compare to a same-weekday local baseline. Treat stale or sparse inputs as unknown instead of normal traffic. Replay a known rush-hour slowdown, a GPS jump near parallel roads and a cluster of devices travelling together.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Enough credible samples arrive for each segment** Map-match samples, aggregate robust window statistics and compare with time-of-day baselines. Accuracy depends on coverage and careful control of correlated observations.
- **Coverage is low or collection is unnecessary** Use historic or public traffic estimates and mark the freshness and confidence. The result may miss incidents that have just started.

## Verification

- Simulate duplicate passengers, stationary points and a genuine traffic delay.
- Verify sparse windows and retention limits produce the expected output.

# Shortest paths with route preprocessing

## Scenario

A regional dispatch app serves repeat route queries between depots. Road geometry changes slowly, while travel-time weights need separate refreshes.

## Failure modes

A shortcut built with one weighting may fail to preserve optimal paths under another. Preserve directed edges, turn restrictions and the path behind each shortcut.

## Explain it simply

Prepare frequent route work ahead of time so each new request checks a smaller set of roads.

## Implementation guidance

Keep a representative unprocessed shortest-path baseline on the same directed graph and compare both travel cost and reconstructed turns. Reuse graph preprocessing across weight changes only with an algorithm designed for that customization, or refresh it according to the weight version. A region with irregular full rebuilds may prefer per-request routing. Test one-way streets, new turn restrictions and a closure that invalidates a formerly optimal shortcut.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The graph is small or changes continuously** Use Dijkstra or an admissible A* over the current graph. Query work grows, but updates stay cheap and semantics remain explicit.
- **Many queries reuse a mostly stable graph** Preprocess shortcuts and choose a customization strategy appropriate for changing weights. Build time, memory and graph update complexity increase.

## Verification

- Compare costs and unpacked routes against a reference solver across random endpoints.
- Test unreachable routes, one-way roads and changed weights after a refresh.

## Sources

- [Contraction Hierarchies, original paper](https://ae.iti.kit.edu/english/1536.php)

## Scenario

A campus shuttle dispatcher must choose from live vehicle locations, including vehicles just across an index cell boundary.

## Failure modes

A fixed cell ring can miss nearby vehicles at borders or in sparse areas. Straight-line proximity and road travel time differ across barriers.

## Explain it simply

Use geographic search to build candidates and road travel time, eligibility and observation freshness for final ranking. Include adjacent cells or expand the search radius until its explicit budget, and expose when that budget prevents a global optimum guarantee. - **Regular grid cells fit update and lookup patterns** Index live locations by cell and expand neighboring rings within a search budget. Resolution trades index churn for candidate volume.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# DNS TTL and service cutover

## Scenario

A service moves to a new endpoint. Some clients may continue reaching the old origin after the record is updated.

## Failure modes

A lower TTL cannot shorten records already cached. Negative caching and long-lived connections can delay recovery or rollback.

## Explain it simply

Keep both endpoints working during the move because some clients remember the old address for a while.

## Implementation guidance

Before a cutover, lower the relevant TTL early enough for cached records with the old TTL to expire and plan for cached negative lookups. TTL governs normal cache freshness. A resolver that implements serve-stale may return expired data when it cannot refresh its answer, and an existing connection can outlive any DNS cache entry. Keep both endpoints contract-compatible while clients migrate and monitor actual traffic reaching each. Test a resolver still holding the old answer, an upstream lookup failure and a client with a reused connection before retiring the old origin.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A migration can be planned and both origins can operate** Lower TTL well ahead, keep both endpoints compatible and compare traffic before retiring the old one. Operating two origins adds temporary cost and synchronization needs.
- **Endpoint ownership and routing can be controlled without DNS churn** Change traffic behind a stable load balancer and use DNS for the stable boundary. The load balancer becomes an operational dependency.

## Verification

- Measure resolver behavior from representative locations during a dry run.
- Test failback with stale records and preexisting connections.

## Sources

- [RFC 1034 Domain Names](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# HTTP validators and cache freshness

## Scenario

A mobile client repeatedly downloads a large public catalog while private account details travel through the same gateway.

## Failure modes

Freshness directives and validators serve different purposes. A missing variant key can mix languages, encodings or users, and returning 304 cannot substitute for authorization.

## Explain it simply

Let the client ask whether its copy is still current without downloading it again.

## Implementation guidance

Pair a freshness policy with a validator appropriate for the representation. Evaluate authentication and tenant visibility before serving either a full response or a 304, and include representation inputs such as language or encoding in Vary when shared caching is allowed. For sensitive account data choose private or no-store as required. Test the same URL for different users and representations as well as a stale client validator after an update.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The response can be publicly shared** Declare Cache-Control policy, vary by representation inputs and issue stable validators. Long freshness can delay changes unless versioned URLs or invalidation are available.
- **The response is sensitive or user-specific** Choose private caching or no-store according to policy and verify intermediaries match it. Fresh requests can cost additional bytes and work.

## Verification

- Verify 304, 200 after change and the expected headers for two content variants.
- Ensure separately authorized users never share a cached private response.

## Sources

- [RFC 9111 HTTP caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111)
- [RFC 9110 HTTP semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Segmented live streaming latency

## Scenario

A regional esports final needs playback that remains responsive under bursty mobile connections and has a measurable delay target.

## Failure modes

Smaller buffers reduce delay but cause stalls on unstable networks. CDN and player behavior can defeat a format-level latency improvement.

## Explain it simply

Send short pieces through nearby servers and let the player hold enough video to avoid frequent pauses.

## Implementation guidance

Measure from capture to display rather than only segment duration. Tune the player live edge, playlist refresh and CDN behavior together. Compare conventional segmented HLS and a supported low-latency path on unstable connections, capturing rebuffering and startup alongside delay. Offer a sensible fallback for unsupported clients and test origin failover while viewers stay connected.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Stability and broad device support dominate** Use conventional HLS segments, CDN caching and a measured playback buffer. Viewers can sit several segments behind capture.
- **End-to-end latency has a tight target** Use Low-Latency HLS partial segments and verify CDN and player support. Expect more requests and lower tolerance for network jitter.

## Verification

- Measure capture-to-playback latency alongside rebuffering under the same network profile.
- Load-test origin requests and verify the player recovers after a missing part.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Token-bucket rate limiting

## Scenario

A support service sends verification messages. Account and network limits must work consistently across several application replicas.

## Failure modes

Aligned fixed windows allow boundary bursts. A shared counter can race. One client identity can map to many genuine users behind a network gateway.

## Explain it simply

Give each limit a small refillable allowance and reject requests only once that allowance is exhausted.

## Implementation guidance

Pick the resource and identity that must be protected before choosing a rate. At the coordination boundary, atomically compute elapsed time, refill up to burst capacity, and then debit the request if enough tokens remain. Use one time source for a shared bucket. If it moves backward, keep the stored time high-water mark and grant no refill until positive elapsed time returns. Evict an inactive bucket only once recreating it as full is equivalent to retaining it. Define failure behavior separately for each protected action, and use HTTP 429 for requests the limiter actually rejects.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Bursts are acceptable within a defined budget** Implement a token bucket with atomic state and an authoritative clock at the coordination boundary. Distributed state adds latency and loss of the store needs a defined fallback.
- **A strict sliding count is required** Use an exact sliding-window log or choose a counter approximation only if the contract allows estimation. Exact logs can consume per-request storage.

## Verification

- Consume a full idle burst across two replicas and verify elapsed-time refill without a window-boundary bonus.
- Simulate the clock moving backward and verify each identity scope and the intended response when the limiter is unavailable.

## Sources

- [RFC 3290 appendix A, traffic profiles and token buckets](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3290#appendix-A)

# HTTP compression with explicit variants

## Scenario

A static catalog contains hundreds of kilobytes of text, while media assets are already compressed.

## Failure modes

Compressing tiny or already compressed responses can waste CPU. Shared caches need correct variants, and sensitive dynamic responses need a reviewed compression policy.

## Explain it simply

Shrink large text responses when the client can decode them, and avoid doing expensive work for files already compressed.

## Implementation guidance

Choose a minimum response size and supported content types at the response boundary, after measuring CPU versus transferred bytes. Negotiate using Accept-Encoding and preserve shared-cache variants and validator semantics. Keep a policy for responses combining secrets and user-controlled data rather than applying the static-asset setting everywhere. Measure cold and warm compression, confirm that already compressed assets are skipped, and query compressed and identity variants through a cache.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Mostly static text is large enough to benefit** Precompress assets or use controlled gzip or Brotli with correct Vary behavior. Build storage or runtime CPU is traded for transfer size.
- **Inputs mix already compressed media or sensitive reflected content** Use selective compression and pick conservative rules at the response boundary. Some responses remain larger to avoid cost or unwanted leakage.

## Verification

- Verify headers, decoding and cache behavior for two supported encodings.
- Measure compressed bytes and CPU under realistic payload sizes.

## Sources

- [RFC 9110 HTTP semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Server-sent events for one-way updates

## Scenario

A report generator streams progress to the browser while the user can still submit commands through ordinary HTTP requests.

## Failure modes

Reconnects can create gaps or duplicates without IDs. Proxy buffering hides updates, and unbounded replay or buffers hurt slow clients.

## Explain it simply

Keep a one-way feed open while work runs and let it resume from the last event the browser received.

## Implementation guidance

Assign progress events stable IDs and use Last-Event-ID to replay later events within a bounded window. When that cursor is too old, send current report state with the matching high-water event ID, then replay newer changes before continuing live delivery. Capture state and cursor at the same consistency boundary so concurrent progress cannot disappear between them. Disable intermediary buffering where needed, send heartbeats compatible with idle timeout, and cap buffers for slow clients. Recognize repeated event IDs when applying updates.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Delivery is primarily server-to-client** Use EventSource with stable event IDs, reconnect policy and a bounded history or snapshot. Browser and proxy timeout behavior needs practical testing.
- **The protocol requires frequent bidirectional traffic** Choose a WebSocket or explicit request-response interactions based on message semantics. Additional connection state and backpressure must be managed.

## Verification

- Disconnect mid-stream and ensure reconnect resumes or returns a fresh snapshot.
- Expire the replay cursor, write an update during the snapshot handoff and verify that the final browser state includes it.
- Test proxy buffering and slow readers under the chosen size limits.

## Sources

- [WHATWG server-sent events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)
- [RFC 6455 WebSocket Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# WebSocket presence and reconnect

## Scenario

A collaboration room wants users to see who is online and typing even when switches between mobile and Wi-Fi interrupt connections.

## Failure modes

A transport connection can become half-open. Multiple devices need aggregation and an old disconnect can overwrite a newer session.

## Explain it simply

Use an open channel for updates and expire a session when it stops checking in.

## Implementation guidance

Assign each connection a distinct identity so an older disconnect cannot erase a newer session for the same user. Heartbeats renew a bounded lease and a disconnect updates that connection alone. Aggregate across a user’s devices before displaying presence. On reconnect, send a versioned snapshot or sequence-consistent replay. Test half-open Wi-Fi, two devices, and an expired connection whose event arrives after the newer session opens.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Updates are frequent or bidirectional** Use WebSockets with heartbeat, lease expiration and reconnect snapshot or replay. Long-lived connections require backpressure, routing and capacity planning.
- **Updates are infrequent or travel only server-to-client** Use bounded polling or server-sent events with a fresh snapshot on reconnect. Polling increases round trips and SSE is a one-way channel.

## Verification

- Test abrupt link loss, reconnect and overlapping sessions.
- Apply slow-client backpressure and assert connections do not accumulate unbounded data.

## Sources

- [RFC 6455 WebSocket Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)
- [WHATWG server-sent events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Streaming transforms with bounded memory

## Scenario

An export utility reads a multi-gigabyte file on a machine with limited memory and produces a second file.

## Failure modes

Collecting all chunks in an array defeats streaming. Decoding independently at each chunk can split multibyte characters and a failed output may appear complete.

## Explain it simply

Read and write one manageable piece at a time, and only publish the finished result.

## Implementation guidance

Use a streaming decoder that carries partial multibyte state between chunks. Bound the largest individual record as well as buffer sizes. Let a slow sink backpressure the producer and publish the output only after the whole pipeline completes. Test split multibyte characters and an interrupted write under a small memory budget.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The transform can preserve limited state per chunk** Use a streaming parser and backpressure-aware pipeline with an atomic final output. Chunk boundaries, resource cleanup and late errors need targeted tests.
- **The transform needs a global ordering or aggregation** Use external sort, bounded partitioning or a database-backed intermediate result. I/O and temporary storage increase to keep memory bounded.

## Verification

- Process an input larger than available RAM and record memory peaks.
- Inject a partial multibyte value, malformed record and output failure.

## Sources

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Cache stampede and prewarming

## Scenario

A university publishes a schedule at a known hour. The first requests would otherwise recompute the same large schedule from the database.

## Failure modes

Identical misses multiply origin queries. Warming too early can publish stale data. Request coalescing is per process unless the coordination boundary covers other instances.

## Explain it simply

Prepare the popular result before the rush and have simultaneous requests share one refresh.

## Implementation guidance

Use the versioned cache key as the single-flight scope. Set a bounded wait for followers and keep ownership and freshness limits explicit across processes. Controlled fallback can serve stale data within the agreed budget after a refresh fails. Observe simultaneous expiry with a delayed or stuck refresher, and verify how a former owner completing after lease expiry is handled.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A predictable event and safe public data** Prewarm versioned content before the surge and set expiry according to staleness policy. Operational timing matters and the final update may require a second warmup.
- **Misses recur unpredictably and stale data has defined bounds** Coalesce refreshes, jitter expiries and serve bounded stale content where acceptable. Adds coordination and stale data must remain visibly within its contract.

## Verification

- Send a burst at expiration and assert origin requests stay under the intended bound.
- Simulate a failed refresh and verify timeouts, fallback behavior and maximum staleness.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Profiling before performance optimization

## Scenario

A command line import tool is perceived as slow, but elapsed time could come from I/O, parsing or contention.

## Failure modes

Microbenchmarks of the wrong function can improve a metric without changing user latency. Cold-start and warm-state behavior may differ.

## Explain it simply

Find where the operation spends time before changing how it works, then measure the whole task again.

## When not to use

Start with the slow workflow and split elapsed time into parsing, storage, dependency waits and local work. A CPU profile is a poor fit for throughput stalls with idle CPU. Measure waiting and queue occupancy first. Record representative workload, warm-up, cache state and resource usage, then compare the end-to-end latency and memory after tuning.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A representative slow workload can be reproduced** Measure an end-to-end baseline, then profile CPU, allocation or blocked time as appropriate. Profiles have overhead and need representative data.
- **The issue occurs only intermittently in a running service** Add narrowly scoped latency and dependency signals before high-overhead profiling. The first measurements may reveal only where to investigate next.

## Verification

- Compare before and after under the same dataset and environment.
- Verify correctness, tail latency and resource trade-offs did not regress.

## Sources

- [Node.js guide to profiling applications](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/profiling)

# N+1 queries and bounded batching

## Scenario

A report lists 50 fields and loads the most recent note for each field with a separate request.

## Failure modes

Joining unbounded relations can expand rows dramatically. Shared caches can leak authorization-sensitive data across requests.

## Explain it simply

Fetch related details for the current page together, then attach them to the right items.

## Implementation guidance

Capture query count in the real report path. Fetch the latest note for all visible field IDs in a scoped batch, or join only the relation needed by each row. Map results by ID and preserve ordering and missing notes. Keep caches request-local where access differs by account and verify that doubling visible fields does not double queries or reveal another tenant’s note.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A page needs a bounded set of related rows** Use a join, eager loading or batched keyed fetch with stable mapping. Result shape and payload size require verification.
- **Optional relationships are large or often unused** Fetch them on demand with independent pagination and a request-specific batching layer. Extra calls remain possible but loaded data stays proportional to use.

## Verification

- Assert query counts stay bounded as page size increases.
- Verify ordering, missing related rows and separate authorization contexts.

# Queue capacity and latency budgeting

## Scenario

A file processing service drains 50 jobs per minute, yet during a promotion receives more than 80 for an extended period.

## Failure modes

An unlimited buffer turns overload into latency and memory growth. Mean service time misses tail impact and heterogeneous job sizes.

## Explain it simply

Set how much work can wait and track whether workers can keep up for the periods that matter.

## Worked example

A service accepting 80 jobs and completing 50 each minute grows its backlog by about 30 jobs a minute while those rates hold. Choose a cap from acceptable queueing time, deadlines and memory. Measure oldest-job age and service times by job class. Stop arrivals after a controlled burst and compare actual drain time and rejection behavior with the plan.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Demand spikes are short and completion can lag briefly** Use a bounded queue and measure time-to-drain against expected bursts. Users may wait, and queue growth needs admission limits.
- **Demand stays above safe service capacity** Scale the measured bottleneck or reject/defer work within explicit service policies. Scaling the wrong stage leaves the bottleneck in place.

## Verification

- Measure arrival, completion and age under a representative burst.
- Verify predictable degradation and bounded storage during sustained overload.

## Sources

- [Google SRE on handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- [MIT Operations Research, distributional Little’s law](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/19154c66-e8bf-47ec-8ba7-fbe4e0345ff3)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Virtual waiting rooms for traffic spikes

## Scenario

Twenty thousand alumni request a limited ticket inventory at opening time. The payment and inventory path can accept a capped arrival rate.

## Failure modes

Browser refreshes can bypass naive queues, and a queue token can be reused if not scoped. A late checkout must not hold inventory indefinitely.

## Explain it simply

Give arrivals a stable place in line and admit only as many as checkout can handle.

## Architecture notes

Admit from an authoritative queue using observed inventory and checkout throughput. A time-limited admission identity should preserve one place across refreshes and remain separate from a booking hold. Define whether an expired pass can rejoin. Exercise multiple tabs for one shopper and a sudden reduction in admission capacity.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Temporary arrival rate greatly exceeds safe capacity** Use a server-managed queue, scoped queue token and measured admission budget. Users wait and operational fairness rules must be clearly defined.
- **Demand is predictable and a queue would add friction** Apply capacity controls or scheduled reservations with clear per-user limits. The approach depends on forecasts and can still require a fallback.

## Verification

- Load-test admission, refresh, reconnect and queue token reuse protections.
- Check transparent handling of sold-out events and abandoned admissions.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Preference updates and deferred changes

## Scenario

A team digest worker schedules emails in advance. A user turns off the digest while messages are already queued.

## Failure modes

The settings screen can show the new value before queued notifications honor it. A settings cache can republish an older preference after concurrent updates.

## Explain it simply

Save the setting and recheck it immediately before sending anything it controls.

## Implementation guidance

Persist consent and its revision with the authoritative preference update, then check policy again at dispatch. A scheduled job can carry its original revision for diagnostics while eligibility depends on current consent and purpose. Define when a send is authorized relative to a revocation. For example, serialize the preference change and the dispatch claim on the same record, then skip previously queued work that has not been claimed. A provider call from a prior claim can still be in flight. Make the product promise match the handoff boundary and use provider cancellation only where it is supported.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A preference forbids a later external action** Persist an authoritative version, acknowledge the save and recheck at dispatch. Each delivery may require a fresh read or a versioned revocation path.
- **A preference only changes low-risk local presentation** Use local state with eventual synchronization and a documented conflict rule. Devices may briefly show different views.

## Verification

- Revoke consent after enqueue and before dispatch authorization, and verify the provider receives no send request.
- Race revocation against an in-flight handoff and verify the reported outcome follows the documented boundary.
- Race cross-device updates and verify the final saved value is visible.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# User feedback during asynchronous workflows

## Scenario

A document upload is accepted immediately but malware scanning and indexing finish later. The user can navigate away and return to the same job.

## Failure modes

Showing success before required checks finish creates a false promise. Polling aggressively can overload the service and a stuck job can leave users without recovery.

## Explain it simply

Tell users the work was received, show what is still pending and give them a way to recover if it stalls.

## Implementation guidance

Return an operation reference on acceptance and persist a status available after reload or reconnect. Distinguish pending, completed, failed and expired and expose a next action for each. Bound polling with a server hint or backoff. Test losing the initial response and reopening or safely retrying a stalled job from another tab.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Completion is delayed but progress is observable** Show a durable operation ID and stable pending, complete and failed states with bounded polling or notifications. Clients need consistent status and clear retry affordances.
- **The user needs a final confirmation before proceeding** Wait within a clear deadline and present pending or recoverable failure when the result is not yet known. The interaction can be slower, but uncertainty stays explicit.

## Verification

- Leave and reopen the screen while the job is pending and verify consistent status.
- Test repeated clicks, long-running jobs and an actionable failed state.

## Sources

- [Azure asynchronous request-reply pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/async-request-reply)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Feature flags and safe rollout

## Scenario

A team enables a redesigned export process for a small cohort and wants to disable it when error rates rise.

## Failure modes

Random assignment per request produces inconsistent user experience. Cached flags can delay shutdown and unretired flags create conflicting paths.

## Explain it simply

Turn the feature on for a steady group first and give operators a clear way to disable it.

## Edge cases

Choose assignment by stable identity and define defaults for missing configuration and stale decisions. If a flag selects code that writes new data, verify old readers and rollback before enabling it. Exercise the same identity across replicas and disable the flag during work. Give the flag an owner and a retirement condition.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Behavior is safe to gate and effects are reversible** Use deterministic targeting, documented fallback, rollout metrics and a removal owner. Both branches need coverage while the flag exists.
- **State changes are irreversible or schema-dependent** Plan compatibility and explicit data transitions before enabling flags that select writers. A flag rollback may not revert data already written.

## Verification

- Verify stable assignment across restarts and flag-provider outages.
- Test disabling after real writes and confirm the rollback contract.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Shuffle semantics and perceived variety

## Scenario

A fitness app has a six-entry offline playlist. One user expects every order to be equally likely. Another wants fewer runs of the same performer. Decide which behavior the control promises before choosing the algorithm. Keep the entire set of queue entries in the result, even if two entries refer to the same track.

## Failure modes

Random sort comparators can give different results for the same pair and do not meet the ordering contract of a sort. Sorting by a random key assigned once per entry is a different technique, with tie semantics and a sort cost to account for. Uniform draws can legitimately cluster. Forcing separation changes the output distribution, while silently discarding a repeated track changes the playlist. Rebuilding the queue on resume can replay or skip entries.

## Explain it simply

A fair draw can put similar tracks next to each other. A variety mode can spread those tracks out while keeping every track. The right option depends on whether equal chances or fewer repetitions matter to the listener.

## When not to use

Use a uniform shuffle for a statistical experiment or a control that promises equal odds per ordering. Artist-aware ordering serves a different preference and can exclude most permutations. If the user asks for only the next item or a recent-play cooldown, define that smaller behavior before building a full artist-aware queue. Specify separately what resuming and explicitly reshuffling do to playback progress.

## Implementation guidance

For a full uniform shuffle, copy the queue and iterate backward from its final index to index one. At each position i, choose j independently and uniformly from the inclusive range zero through i, then swap the two entries. With an unbiased bounded draw, the construction gives each permutation the same probability and takes linear time. Inject the bounded draw for repeatable tests. Choose a source appropriate to the product and use a bounded drawing API or rejection sampling when reduction would bias the range.

For an artist-aware mode, group entries by stable artist identity, randomize within each group, then choose a substantial remaining group different from the last one when possible. A common policy chooses the largest eligible group and uses a random draw to break ties. When only the last group remains, emit its remaining entries under the declared fallback. Preserve a unique identity per queue entry. State how collaborations or missing artist metadata are grouped so the rule uses stable inputs.

## Worked example

With two entries each from artists A, B and C, A A B B C C is a legitimate uniform result. A B C A B C is a valid variety result. A single fixed run can demonstrate the listener experience, while exhaustive bounded draws on three entries can verify the Fisher–Yates permutation mapping. The repository's six-track demonstration compares these goals with a random-comparator baseline using a repeatable seed. Its repeat counts illustrate one sample, not a statistical evaluation of sorting behavior.

Spotify Engineering describes a Fewer Repeats method that scores multiple random candidate orders by how recently tracks were heard, then picks the highest-scoring order. The artist-grouping rule here is a standalone design choice for products that want to reduce back-to-back artists. The published Spotify example supports the distinction between statistical randomness and listener perception.

## Architecture notes

Place order generation in a pure queue-building policy when separate service ownership or deployment is unnecessary. The playback controller should consume queue entries and advance one cursor. When resume must preserve a session, persist ordered entry IDs and progress together, or retain the seed, algorithm version and immutable source revision needed to reconstruct exactly that order. Apply playlist edits through a defined queue revision, with any rescheduling limited to the unplayed portion unless the listener starts a new shuffle. If the variety rule covers the transition across an edit, pass the last played artist into the new ordering policy. After playing A, the remaining entries A and B should start with B even though either order has zero repeats within the remaining queue alone.

## Edge cases

For n total entries with m from the dominant artist, n - m other entries create at most n - m + 1 gaps. Thus at least max(0, 2m - n - 1) dominant adjacent pairs are unavoidable. With four A entries and only B and C as separators, at least one A adjacency remains. Also cover empty and singleton queues, all entries from one artist, two queue entries pointing to one track, and metadata changes between shuffle and resume. For the all-one-artist case, preserve every entry and make the fallback explicit.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The product promises equal odds for each permutation** Use Fisher–Yates with an unbiased bounded random integer at each step. Clusters are legitimate and tests should not reject them.
- **The product prioritizes perceived variety** Schedule by groups with an explicit repeat rule and a documented fallback for skew, using random tie breaks. Constrained schedules sacrifice permutation uniformity.

## Verification

- Prove the output is a permutation of queue-entry IDs and leaves the input order intact, including two entries that refer to the same track.
- For Fisher–Yates, exhaust all bounded draws for a three-entry queue and observe all six permutations exactly once.
- Check an interleavable queue, a single artist, and an excess of one artist against the documented repeat limit.
- When resume must preserve the order, restart between two tracks and verify the next queue-entry ID is unchanged.
- If variety is promised across an edit, verify the next artist against the last played artist and preserve every unplayed entry.

## Sources

- [NIST dictionary entry on Fisher–Yates](https://www.nist.gov/dads/HTML/fisherYatesShuffle.html)
- [ECMAScript Array.prototype.sort and consistent comparator requirements](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-array.prototype.sort)
- [Spotify Engineering on perceived randomness](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/11/shuffle-making-random-feel-more-human)

## Related decisions

- [Persistent playback queue and resume behavior](persistent-playback-queue.md)

- [Property-based tests for invariants](../testing/property-based-testing.md)

# Persistent playback queue and resume behavior

## Scenario

An audiobook app mixes clips for a practice session. A phone restart should resume the expected next clip, even if the source library changed.

## Failure modes

Re-shuffling on every resume can replay and skip clips. Array indices can point at a different item after deletion. Identical track IDs can represent separate queue entries.

## Explain it simply

Save the session's ordered queue and current position, so resuming continues the same session.

## Architecture notes

Use distinct queue-entry identities even where two entries refer to the same track. Persist ordered entries and the next entry under one queue revision. A replayable seed needs an algorithm version and stable inputs as well. Exercise resume with a removed source track and repeated queue entries, and check that the cursor advances once.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Users expect the current sequence to survive app restart** Persist queue item identities and progress together, and define how deleted items are skipped. Snapshot state adds storage and requires a versioned format.
- **Sessions are disposable or deliberately restart the order** Persist minimal state and explicitly signal that resume starts a new sequence. Restart is cheap but can feel like lost progress.

## Verification

- Restart after repeated IDs and verify the next distinct entry is preserved.
- Remove the current track during a pause and verify the published resume rule.

# Scheduling across time zones and DST

## Scenario

A volunteer reminder repeats every Sunday at 09:00 in Berlin, while one-off reminders are delivered at a known instant worldwide.

## Failure modes

UTC alone loses intended wall-clock recurrence. Nonexistent and repeated local times can cause missed or duplicate reminders.

## Explain it simply

Save a recurring meeting's local time and named zone so it stays at the intended hour when clocks change.

## Implementation guidance

Store a recurring local time with its named zone and explicit gap and overlap policy. Persist a triggered occurrence with a fixed instant and stable identity. A weekly 09:00 appointment stays at 09:00 through DST even when its UTC time shifts. Test nonexistent spring time, repeated autumn time, and reruns of the same occurrence.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The event recurs at a local wall time** Store local schedule, IANA zone and explicit gap or overlap rules, then compute each occurrence. Timezone rule updates can change future occurrences.
- **The task runs at a fixed elapsed time or known instant** Store and compare an instant and render it in the viewer's preferred zone. The displayed wall time may shift when timezone rules change.

## Verification

- Test spring gaps, fall overlaps and a zone with a non-hour offset.
- Verify job retries cannot create two effects for one logical occurrence.

## Sources

- [RFC 5545 calendar recurrence](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5545)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Circuit breakers for dependency failure

## Scenario

A checkout quote service calls a dependency that intermittently becomes unreachable. Thread pools saturate while failing calls wait.

## Failure modes

A global breaker can suppress healthy endpoints. Half-open probes can stampede, and an inappropriate fallback can misrepresent critical results.

## Explain it simply

Pause most calls while a dependency is failing and make a small controlled probe before accepting traffic again.

## Implementation guidance

Group operations by shared dependency and failure behavior. Define which outcomes count, how many half-open probes may run and what fallback remains truthful. If isolated incidents already fit a deadline and retry budget, verify that before introducing state. Fault one operation and confirm a healthy peer stays available during recovery.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Repeated dependency failure can exhaust caller resources** Use per-operation breaker state with thresholds, timeouts and bounded half-open probes. Tuning is nontrivial and the fallback must preserve the product contract.
- **Failures are rare or a bounded timeout is sufficient** Prefer explicit deadlines and a small retry budget, observing recovery first. Fewer moving parts but callers still experience individual failures.

## Verification

- Simulate failing and recovered dependencies and verify controlled half-open traffic.
- Verify a breaker for one dependency leaves independent paths available.

## Sources

- [Azure circuit breaker pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker)
- [AWS timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

# Poison messages and dead-letter handling

## Scenario

An order worker encounters a malformed event. Retrying continuously blocks later orders in the same queue.

## Failure modes

A dead-letter queue without ownership loses work silently. Blind redrive repeats harm, and queue TTL can expire faster than investigation.

## Explain it simply

Move consistently failing work aside, retain enough information to fix it and replay only when it can succeed.

## Implementation guidance

Store a stable message ID, first-seen time, attempt count and sanitized reason. Set alerting and retention against a known owner’s response budget. Redrive a small verified cohort after a fix and keep its effects idempotent. Exercise restart during routing, a malformed event between valid work and a replay of a still-poisoned message.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A single message can block progress or exhaust retries** Move failed work to a monitored dead-letter queue with reason, attempt and stable ID. Operators need a retention window and an intentional redrive workflow.
- **Strict order prevents skipping work** Pause that partition and resolve the blocking event before continuing, with bounded isolation. Throughput for that partition falls until the incident is handled.

## Verification

- Deliver a persistent failure and verify unrelated work proceeds as intended.
- Redrive an already applied event and verify the consumer does not repeat the effect.

## Sources

- [Amazon SQS dead-letter queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)
- [RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements and confirms](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms)
