<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Recovery objectives and restore verification

## Scenario

A grants database is backed up each night. A failed primary could interrupt the submission deadline and lose changes accepted earlier that day.

## Failure modes

A backup success notification does not prove restorability. Missing credentials, corrupt restores and dependencies outside the backup can lengthen recovery.

## Explain it simply

Decide how much data and time you can afford to lose, then rehearse restoring a representative system.

## Verification details

Derive backup frequency and recovery mechanics from tolerable data loss and duration. Inventory credentials, keys, configuration and external dependencies required for reopening. Restore a representative snapshot to isolation, check record integrity and accept a new submission end to end. Measure time from declaration and identify the last recoverable write.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The acceptable recovery point is similar to backup cadence** Use tested snapshots with a documented restore order and separate access controls. Snapshots leave a gap between backups.
- **A narrow recovery point or short outage is required** Add point-in-time recovery or managed standby and run regular failover drills. Storage, coordination and operational overhead grow.

## Verification

- Restore into isolation and check representative records and permission paths.
- Measure elapsed time and lost acknowledged changes against the stated objectives.

## Sources

- [PostgreSQL backup and restore](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup.html)
- [Google SRE on data integrity](https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Distributed tracing and sampling

## Scenario

A search path spans an API, a cache and a remote ranking worker. Tail latency sometimes rises while aggregate metrics look stable.

## Failure modes

Missing propagation breaks traces. Parent-only sampling can miss rare errors, and labels with user data can leak information.

## Explain it simply

Follow a request through the system and measure where its time was spent.

## Architecture notes

Propagate trace context across synchronous and queued stages, with spans where ownership or waiting changes. Keep sensitive search input out of attributes and cap cardinality. Choose sampling that keeps enough error traces to explain tail failures. Reproduce a downstream failure and verify context retention across handoff and retry.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Work spans independently observed components** Propagate standard trace context and instrument defined boundaries with safe tags. Span collection and sampling add overhead and require retention controls.
- **One local process is the only bottleneck** Start with latency metrics and targeted profiling before adding cross-service tracing. Metrics show distribution but provide less detail for a single operation.

## Verification

- Trace a request across a queued job and ensure privacy-sensitive inputs are absent.
- Induce a tail-latency problem and verify sampled traces can show the cause.

## Sources

- [W3C Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/)
- [OpenTelemetry tracing concepts](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Graceful shutdown and work draining

## Scenario

A service receives a deployment termination signal while a long upload and queued jobs are running.

## Failure modes

An unregister step can race incoming traffic. Termination during an acknowledged but uncommitted stage can lose work or cause duplicate processing.

## Explain it simply

Stop admitting new work, finish what fits in the shutdown window and leave the rest ready to resume.

## Implementation guidance

Mark the instance unready, stop admitting work and let in-flight requests reach their durable boundary until a deadline. Reschedule work that cannot finish and make the next attempt safe. Close shared resources after workers stop using them. Rehearse termination with accepted, committing and queued operations, then repeat with an abrupt kill.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The platform gives a timed shutdown grace period** Mark unready, drain requests, honor cancellation and requeue work before deadline. Long operations may still need checkpoints and idempotency.
- **Fast abrupt termination is expected under failures** Design durable boundaries and recovery independent of shutdown hooks. More persistent state is needed, even though planned drains can reduce interruption.

## Verification

- Terminate during a request and during durable processing, then verify behavior on restart.
- Assert deadline expiration leaves no indefinitely held lease.

## Sources

- [Kubernetes pod lifecycle and termination](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# End-to-end deadlines and timeouts

## Scenario

An address lookup becomes slow while an API gateway allows a single two-second budget for checkout validation.

## Failure modes

A per-attempt timer can exceed the caller's overall budget. A timeout that abandons only the result can leave database and socket work running.

## Explain it simply

Give each downstream call part of the time the user can wait, and stop work the user no longer needs when possible.

## Implementation guidance

Compute time remaining from the caller deadline and fit connect, read and retry budgets inside it. Allow the caller enough time to report a clear error. Propagate cancellation when supported and observe residual resource use. Simulate no connection, a connection that accepts without replying, and completion just after expiration.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Calls are synchronous and the caller needs a response** Propagate a deadline, set connect and read budgets, and cancel work when supported. Aggressive deadlines may increase retries or visible failures.
- **Work can outlive the original interaction** Accept it durably and provide progress or later completion with an explicit deadline. Async work needs reconciliation, persistence and a way to check status.

## Verification

- Hang a dependency and assert response returns within the deadline.
- Verify client cancellation releases capacity and retries respect the remaining budget.

## Sources

- [AWS timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
- [gRPC deadlines](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Stateful failover and split-brain prevention

## Scenario

A co-op tournament server keeps a match's last confirmed state. If the active node disappears, players should reconnect without losing confirmed moves.

## Failure modes

A missing heartbeat means loss of reachability. The original leader can return while a new one writes. Async replication can lose updates that were acknowledged.

## Explain it simply

Keep a recoverable copy and ensure only the current leader can move the match forward.

## Implementation guidance

State which acknowledgements are durable under the replication mode. The storage path must enforce fencing or consensus ownership when leadership changes. Measure election and client recovery separately. Exercise a network split with both nodes running, then prove the former primary can rejoin without overwriting later acknowledged state.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Recovery time and confirmed-state loss are tightly bounded** Replicate state with explicit acknowledgement rules and use a trusted lease or fencing epoch enforced by storage. Stronger guarantees add coordination and latency.
- **Some recent noncritical state is disposable** Restore from periodic checkpoints and communicate the recovery point. Recovery is simpler but the latest state may be missing.

## Verification

- Partition old and new leaders and verify stale writes are rejected.
- Measure recovery time and acknowledged data loss during failover drills.

## Sources

- [Raft consensus paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
- [PostgreSQL high availability and standby servers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Readiness, liveness and startup checks

## Scenario

A web process warms an index before accepting requests. A short database outage should temporarily remove it from traffic when requests cannot be served.

## Failure modes

Treating every dependency outage as a liveness problem causes restart loops. Too-short startup thresholds can keep slow instances from ever becoming ready.

## Explain it simply

Check separately whether the process is alive and whether it can safely serve real requests right now.

## Implementation guidance

Use startup checks during warm-up, readiness to decide whether an instance should receive its real traffic, and liveness for a process that cannot recover. A remote outage can fail readiness without restarting healthy processes. Test a slow initial index build, a temporary dependency outage and graceful removal from traffic.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A long startup and recoverable readiness failures are normal** Use distinct startup, liveness and readiness checks tied to real capabilities. Thresholds and dependency criteria must be observed under load.
- **A simple process reliably starts and serves immediately** Use a minimal health strategy with a bounded shutdown and a test of the real route. Simpler probes provide fewer diagnostic distinctions.

## Verification

- Delay startup and verify no traffic arrives before readiness.
- Simulate a dependency outage and verify the chosen restart and drain behavior.

## Sources

- [Kubernetes liveness, readiness and startup probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)
- [Kubernetes deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Retry budgets, backoff and jitter

## Scenario

A dashboard calls a failing permissions service through two API layers. Each layer can retry independently while the user waits for one response.

## Failure modes

Nested retries multiply calls. Retrying deterministic errors wastes capacity, and synchronized attempts create another load spike. Side effects require reuse of logical identity.

## Explain it simply

Try short-lived failures again a limited number of times and spread the attempts out.

## Implementation guidance

Choose one retry owner and propagate its time or attempt budget down. Retry known transient errors with jitter and a cap, reuse the logical key for side effects and surface deterministic failures promptly. Record attempt count per user operation to catch multiplicative retries. Exercise a lost successful acknowledgement, synchronized callers and an outage longer than their deadline.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The operation is safe to repeat within the request deadline** Retry at one responsible layer with capped exponential backoff, jitter and an explicit attempt budget. Some transient failures will be surfaced when the budget runs out.
- **A timeout may hide a completed non-idempotent side effect** Use a stable operation key, check status, or surface a recoverable pending result. The workflow needs durable state and reconciliation.

## Verification

- Inject transient and permanent errors and count total downstream calls.
- Verify backoff does not extend the caller's deadline and handles cancellation.

## Sources

- [AWS timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
- [AWS exponential backoff and jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Mixed-version deployment compatibility

## Scenario

A background worker starts writing a field before every old API instance has drained. A rollout may be paused for hours.

## Failure modes

New required fields or changed enum assumptions break old readers. Rollback after destructive migration can restore code that cannot read the data.

## Explain it simply

Make old and new versions compatible while they run side by side, then remove obsolete shapes after the rollout.

## Edge cases

Constrain writers to data understood by every current reader and keep new reading behavior compatible with both versions. Tie switching to verified readiness or data revision instead of an arbitrary time after deploy. Exercise old writer/new reader and new writer/old reader pairs. Pause the rollout with both versions active and verify the rollback still reads data they produced.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Multiple versions will run during deploy** Use expand, migrate and contract with tolerant readers and version-checked writers. The compatibility phase needs measured completion and temporary extra code.
- **A genuinely isolated replacement is possible** Deploy into versioned storage, quiesce writers and switch readers at a verified boundary. The cutover can introduce downtime or state synchronization cost.

## Verification

- Run old and new writer-reader combinations against representative old and new data.
- Practice rollback across every boundary where the change is advertised as reversible.

## Sources

- [Stripe Engineering online migrations](https://stripe.com/blog/online-migrations)
- [Kubernetes deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Service-level objectives and burn alerts

## Scenario

A file editor needs to know whether save failures are frequent enough to slow feature rollout. Server CPU rises on unrelated tasks.

## Failure modes

Measuring instance uptime can miss failed saves. Low traffic and short windows can make ratios noisy.

## Explain it simply

Track whether users can do what they need and use failures over time to decide when to prioritize reliability.

## Worked example

Define a save SLI from eligible user-visible requests and a success deadline. With a 99.9% target, a 1% failure ratio corresponds to ten times the allowed fraction. Use short and long windows to distinguish rapid budget loss and sustained burn, and document sparse traffic. Show that injected save failures can trip the alert while an unrelated CPU spike does not.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A user outcome has stable success and eligibility signals** Define a request-based SLI with an explicit window and alert on fast and sustained error-budget burn. Eligibility and low-volume behavior require careful definitions.
- **A normal interaction cannot be measured from server logs** Add representative synthetic or client instrumentation and compare its coverage. Synthetic paths may miss browser, geography and account-specific conditions.

## Verification

- Replay a known outage and verify alerts and eligible-event counts.
- Confirm benign maintenance and a real user-visible failure have the intended accounting.

## Sources

# Structured logs and request correlation

## Scenario

Customer support sees a sporadic checkout failure across an API and worker but cannot correlate their messages.

## Failure modes

Free-form messages are hard to query. Logging request bodies can expose personal data. User-controlled IDs should not be trusted as diagnostic identity.

## Explain it simply

Give each request a safe tracking ID and record the facts needed to find where it failed.

## Implementation guidance

Emit a stable event name and fields for operation, result, stage and a validated request or trace ID. Propagate IDs before asynchronous handoff rather than copying whole requests to logs. Audit retention, sampling and redaction rules. Deliberately fail a checkout and reconstruct its path across service and worker events without revealing payment or personal values.

# Object-level authorization and tenancy

## Scenario

An invoice API returns a single invoice by ID. Staff in each organization may only access invoices owned by that organization.

## Failure modes

UI filtering does not enforce permission. A lookup by ID followed by an unscoped update may leave gaps on secondary paths or exports.

## Explain it simply

Check whether the requester may access the exact record each time the service reads or changes it.

## Implementation guidance

At the data boundary query by object identity and the caller’s authorized workspace scope, then check permission for the requested action. Apply the same policy to reads, mutations and exports. An invoice number identifies a record while membership governs access. Verify with two organizations that another workspace cannot read or mutate the invoice even with its number.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Permissions align to a simple owner or tenant** Scope lookups and mutations to the caller's allowed tenant and enforce role checks for actions. Scopes must be applied to bulk, export and background paths too.
- **Objects have delegated membership or shared ACLs** Centralize reusable policy evaluation with clear deny-by-default and membership freshness behavior. Policy caching and delegation expand the test matrix.

## Verification

- Verify a same-role user in another tenant receives no object on read or update.
- Test missing membership, revoked sharing and bulk operation scoping.

# Content Security Policy for browser applications

## Scenario

An application embeds a limited set of script and frame providers, then wants to restrict unexpected page resources.

## Failure modes

Overbroad source expressions weaken protection. Enforcing a strict policy without inventory can silently break production pages.

## Explain it simply

Choose which resources the browser is allowed to run and first check how the policy affects existing pages.

## Implementation guidance

Inventory actual script, style, frame and fetch dependencies before tightening the policy. Review report-only data where appropriate, then verify authenticated pages under actual enforcement. Use per-response nonces for approved inline scripts or hashes for stable inline code. Remove dependencies asking for broad directives when possible instead of making them defaults.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **An application can inventory and control most resources** Use a narrowly scoped policy with nonces or hashes where appropriate and monitor report-only results before enforcement. Changing libraries can require policy and test updates.
- **Legacy pages must be migrated gradually** Deploy policy per route and prioritize removing dependencies that need broad permissions. Coverage differences need a documented rollout and monitoring plan.

## Verification

- Test primary workflows under the enforced response headers.
- Confirm violations are observable and report handling avoids retaining sensitive URLs.

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Random sources for tokens and product choices

## Scenario

A service produces password reset tokens and also rotates a list of featured articles. The two decisions have different consequences.

## Failure modes

A deterministic or general-purpose source can expose authentication tokens. Modulo reduction can bias selection, even if the input bytes are strong.

## Explain it simply

Use hard-to-guess randomness for access tokens, and select a suitable random source and rule for viewing experiences.

## Implementation guidance

Choose a random source based on predictability risk and distribution requirements. For reset tokens, generate with a platform cryptographic generator and protect the stored verifier with bounded lifetime. A seeded source can reproduce presentation tests. Use a bounded draw designed to preserve fairness where needed and test expiry and token replay separately from the random branch tests.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A secret must resist guessing or prediction** Use the platform cryptographic RNG, scoped lifetime and secure storage or verification. Stronger randomness does not replace rate limiting and authorization.
- **Randomness is for a reproducible test or nonsecurity simulation** Use an explicit seeded test generator and an unbiased selection scheme where needed. Deterministic sequences should remain isolated from security decisions.

## Verification

- Check token generation uses the intended primitive and expiry rules.
- Use deterministic fixtures for distribution-related logic without claiming tests prove unpredictability.

# CSRF protection for browser sessions

## Scenario

A web app uses a session cookie and exposes settings changes through browser forms and JSON endpoints.

## Failure modes

The browser can attach cookies to cross-site requests under some conditions. Read-only endpoints should not change state, and SameSite needs an explicit compatibility assessment.

## Explain it simply

Require proof that a change came from a legitimate session and an intended page of the application.

## Implementation guidance

Identify routes that change state and which credentials the browser can attach automatically. Apply the framework CSRF check to that state-changing path for both form and client-app variants. Choose suitable cookie attributes in addition to that guard. Test legitimate mutations through the real public route and verify that safe methods leave state as it was.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Browser cookies authenticate state-changing requests** Use framework CSRF protection or session-bound tokens, with safe HTTP methods and suitable cookie attributes. Cross-site integrations and token refresh need deliberate support.
- **Authorization uses a non-ambient credential controlled by the client** Verify that cookies or other ambient credentials cannot silently authenticate the same endpoint. CORS configuration and client storage risks still need separate review.

## Verification

- Verify normal and expired-token submissions from the app work as expected.
- Assert a request from an untrusted origin without valid proof cannot change state.

# Parameterized database queries

## Scenario

An internal search endpoint accepts a search term, a sort choice and a page-size value from a request payload.

## Failure modes

Escaping strings manually depends on SQL dialect and encoding. Query parameters bind literals and usually cannot stand in for table or column identifiers.

## Explain it simply

Send values as data and translate each supported sort choice into a known database column.

## Implementation guidance

Bind search values and page limits using the database driver. Map any user-selectable sort column or direction to a finite set of trusted query constructions. Check domain limits and authorization before running the query. Test punctuation in ordinary data, unrecognized sorts and oversized pages while ensuring expected search results remain available.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **User input maps to a comparison value** Use the driver or ORM's bound parameters and keep the SQL structure static. The database API's parameter conventions must remain correct across queries.
- **Users legitimately choose a sort or field name** Map a small allowed enum to trusted query fragments and parameterize values separately. New options require an explicit mapping and tests.

## Verification

- Assert special characters and unusual Unicode remain literal query values.
- Test unknown sort names are rejected and least-privilege permissions cover the intended query.

# Defensive file ingest for user uploads

## Scenario

A portfolio service accepts images and previews them after processing in a background worker.

## Failure modes

Name and MIME hints are user controlled. Very large decoded images can exhaust resources, and serving uploads from an application origin can create unwanted trust.

## Explain it simply

Place incoming files in a restricted area and make them public only after checking they are the kind and size expected.

## Architecture notes

Establish an allowed content policy and limits on uploaded and decoded size. Generate the storage name independently of supplied names and parse in a constrained worker. Publish only after a successful recorded result, using a response or origin policy for untrusted content. Exercise oversized, mislabeled and interrupted inputs and prove that each remains quarantined.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Only a narrow set of file types is required** Allowlist supported formats and bound stored and decoded size; serve from a separate controlled origin. Validation and content transformation can add latency and cost.
- **High-risk documents require isolated processing** Use an isolated worker with constrained permissions, quarantine and explicit result states. Users must see processing status and recoverable failures.

## Verification

- Verify type mismatches, decoded-size limits and failed processing leave objects private.
- Confirm approved files are served with the expected origin and response headers.

# Secret storage, rotation and observability

## Scenario

A scheduled integration uses a vendor key that must be rotated while two deployment versions are active.

## Failure modes

Source control and logs persist long after a deployment. Revoking the old key before new instances load the replacement can cause an outage.

## Explain it simply

Keep credentials in a controlled location and switch to the replacement before retiring the old one when the provider allows it.

## Implementation guidance

Inventory which workloads use each credential and required scope. Stage the replacement before revocation where supported, and test both deployed versions against it. Log key identity and outcomes without secret values. Rehearse emergency revocation and reissue, including a client still holding a credential in an in-memory cache.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A managed workload can use short-lived identity** Prefer workload identity or a scoped token fetched at runtime with explicit expiry. Identity provider availability and refresh handling become important.
- **A vendor accepts only static keys** Store scoped keys outside source, stage safe overlap for rotation and verify revocation. Rotation needs operational ownership and documented recovery.

## Verification

- Rotate in a test environment and verify both the new key and old-key revocation.
- Check logs, dumps and error reports for accidental secret exposure.

## Sources

- [OWASP secrets management](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)

# Authenticating and processing webhooks

## Scenario

A shipping provider notifies the warehouse when a package clears customs. The provider retries callbacks until acknowledged.

## Failure modes

Parsing the body before verification can change signed bytes. Valid events can be delivered more than once or out of order, and unsafe logging may expose secrets.

## Explain it simply

Verify who sent the message before acting, then remember which delivery has already been applied.

## Implementation guidance

Pass the exact request bytes to the provider verifier before acting. Enforce the provider’s freshness policy, then record a stable event or delivery identity at the durability boundary. Acknowledge after the durable acceptance if processing runs out of band. Test secret rotation, tampered content, duplicate valid delivery and an older valid event arriving after newer state.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Provider signing supports timestamped signatures** Use the provider's official verifier on raw bytes and enforce documented replay bounds. Clock drift and secret rotation must remain compatible.
- **A provider lacks acceptable signing** Use a trusted restricted integration channel or reconcile through authenticated polling. Polling increases latency and cannot rely on immediate push delivery.

## Verification

- Test valid delivery, changed body, expired signature and repeated authenticated event.
- Rotate the signing secret and verify the documented overlap and unfamiliar-key behavior.

## Sources

## Scenario

A trial expiry job sets remaining access based on a clock. Tests should check exact expiration and delayed worker starts.

## Failure modes

Sleeping creates slow flaky tests. A mocked clock does not model database time or process scheduling unless the production time source is explicit.

## Explain it simply

Let tests choose the time so they can check what happens just before and just after a deadline.

## Implementation guidance

Identify production time sources that determine eligibility, including scheduler or database clocks if relevant. ## Decision rules

- **The decision can read time through a small seam** Inject a clock and advance it directly in tests. The integration path still needs a check for the production time source.
- **Framework timers drive the real flow** Use supported fake timers with explicit promise and task flushing, plus a narrow real-time smoke test. Clock simulation may differ from distributed time behavior.

## Verification

- Verify before, at and after the boundary without sleeps.

# Controlled fault injection and recovery tests

## Scenario

A worker reserves inventory, then calls a simulated dependency that can fail at multiple points. Each stage should have an observable outcome after restart.

## Failure modes

Tests that only throw before the operation skip ambiguous post-commit failures. Large uncontrolled failures can obscure the expected invariant.

## Explain it simply

Rehearse one failure at a time and check that the system can recover without leaving half-finished work.

## Verification details

Map the durability boundaries between inventory and external calls. Inject one failure immediately before and immediately after each boundary, restart the handler and observe what can be safely replayed or must stay pending. A committed provider effect with a lost acknowledgement is a different case from failure before any effect. Start with bounded fixture experiments with observable invariants.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **A decision has identifiable side-effect boundaries** Inject failures around those boundaries in a controlled integration test and replay recovery. Fixtures must represent durable state and actual retries.
- **A system must withstand infrastructure-level disruption** Use a scoped nonproduction resilience exercise with explicit abort conditions and baseline monitoring. Complex drills are slower and harder to diagnose.

## Verification

- Check interrupted work resumes, rolls back or enters a documented pending state.
- Verify a successful replay preserves the invariant and yields a usable operator signal.

## Sources

- [AWS Well-Architected resilience testing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/test-reliability.html)
- [Google SRE on data integrity](https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Load tests with realistic arrival models

## Scenario

A checkout service meets latency targets with 100 virtual users, but real users arrive independently of current response speed.

## Failure modes

Closed-loop drivers slow their arrivals when the server gets slower. Load generators may saturate or omit failed responses from reports.

## Explain it simply

Send requests at the rate real demand would arrive and measure how long users actually wait.

## Implementation guidance

Use an independent arrival schedule for workloads that keep growing while the server slows. Track dropped starts, generator utilization and errors alongside tail latency, including end-to-end waiting. A closed model can instead reflect a fixed group with realistic think times. Apply the same slowdown to both models and compare arrivals and measured tails to the expected workload.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Production demand arrives independently of server latency** Use an open arrival-rate model, track dropped iterations and include errors and tail latency. The generator needs its own headroom to maintain target arrival rate.
- **Each real user submits the next request only after a result** Use a closed concurrency model with realistic think times and document the model. It can under-represent overload when production arrivals are independent.

## Verification

- Inject a slow stage and verify reported latency includes waiting, failures and dropped work.
- Confirm the generator reached its configured shape at each recorded load point.

## Sources

- [Grafana k6 open and closed models](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/concepts/open-vs-closed/)
- [Google SRE on handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Property-based tests for invariants

## Scenario

A date range utility must normalize arbitrary ranges, merge overlaps and preserve coverage over a bounded interval.

## Failure modes

A property can be true for a broken trivial implementation. Unseeded failures are hard to reproduce and generators can avoid the edge of interest.

## Explain it simply

Check a rule that must hold for many inputs and save the smallest example when the rule fails.

## Worked example

For normalized date ranges, compare input and output coverage on a small discrete reference domain, check sorted nonoverlapping output, and require applying normalization twice to yield the same result. Generate empty, adjacent, nested and extreme ranges. Keep the minimized failure and its seed for replay and add a direct regression even if the generator changes.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **Behavioral invariants or a reference oracle are available** Generate boundary-rich inputs, assert the properties and record reproducible failure seeds. Developers must choose strong properties and constrain test budgets.
- **A narrow product rule has only a few meaningful cases** Start with explicit examples including one failing case and a boundary. Examples are readable but explore fewer combinations.

## Verification

- Introduce a deliberately broken implementation and verify a property fails.
- Replay one reported failure from its seed and preserve it as a regression case.

## Sources

- [fast-check documentation](https://fast-check.dev/docs/introduction/)
- [Hypothesis documentation](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/)

## Related decisions

- [Shuffle semantics and perceived variety](../product/music-shuffle.md)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Focused snapshots for stable outputs

## Scenario

A CLI generates a structured project report whose layout and relative paths are part of its user contract.

## Failure modes

Timestamps, locale and temporary paths make snapshots noisy. Blind regeneration can accept real regressions. Broad snapshots may obscure the critical invariant.

## Explain it simply

Keep a reviewed reference output for stable details and add direct checks for the rules users depend on.

## Implementation guidance

Normalize temporary paths, clocks or locale only where incidental to the contract. Preserve structure and ordering that carry meaning. Pair compact snapshots with direct assertions on invariants a textual diff would hide. Try a harmless environment change that should preserve the snapshot and a required output change that should be caught before accepting updates.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **The serialized output is a meaningful, stable interface** Normalize incidental environment data and approve small, reviewed snapshots. A format change requires updating and reviewing the stored output.
- **Only a few assertions describe the contract** Use focused structural and behavioral assertions instead of storing an entire output. Unexpected layout changes outside those assertions require separate checks.

## Verification

- Run on multiple working directories and assert deterministic normalized output.
- Make a deliberate breaking change and confirm the test highlights it.

## Sources

- [Jest snapshot testing](https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing)
- [Node.js test runner](https://nodejs.org/api/test.html)

<!-- Generated record title. -->
# Choosing test doubles and integration seams

## Scenario

An invoicing service depends on a database and job broker. Mock call assertions pass although a real uniqueness rule rejects the operation.

## Failure modes

Mocking internal call order makes safe refactors brittle. A fake's consistency or encoding can differ from the real dependency.

## Explain it simply

Replace pieces only where needed to control a test, and use the real pieces where their behavior determines correctness.

## Implementation guidance

A fake can model failure timing cheaply, but use the representative real database to test uniqueness and the real broker when durability matters. Assert the invoice state or durable event across that public boundary. A two-writer assertion that passes with an in-memory fake yet fails at the store is evidence to keep the integration case.

<!-- Generated record details. Edit the YAML above and run npm run catalog. -->

## Decision rules

- **An isolated policy has stable inputs and outputs** Test it directly using a small fake or data fixture at an external boundary. A unit test will not prove real database or transport behavior.
- **A transaction, protocol or consistency contract is part of the invariant** Use an integration test with a representative dependency and assert observable outcomes. These tests are more expensive and need controlled setup and teardown.

## Verification

- Demonstrate a meaningful fault the chosen test would catch.
- Confirm a refactor that preserves the public behavior leaves the test valid.

## Sources

- [Martin Fowler, Mocks Aren’t Stubs](https://martinfowler.com/articles/mocksArentStubs.html)
- [pytest fixtures documentation](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/fixtures.html)

# Engineering standards

Start with the invariant, the owner of each piece of state, and an observable check. Respect the project's language and conventions. Read only the guides whose choices change the outcome.

| When the work changes… | Read |
|---|---|
| The first product slice, stack, or delivery plan | [Greenfield planning](standards/greenfield.md) |
| Deployment, domain ownership, or independent scaling | [Architecture](standards/architecture.md) |
| Folder layout, file naming, or package boundaries | [Project structure](standards/structure.md) |
| Placement, reuse, interfaces, or separation of responsibilities | [Modularity and reuse](standards/modularity.md) |
| Dependencies, duplication, abstraction, or maintenance cost | [Code principles](standards/code-principles.md), [Dependencies](standards/dependencies.md) |
| Endpoints, request validation, errors, or compatibility | [API contracts](standards/api.md) |
| Schema, indexing, transactions, or migrations | [Data and storage](standards/data.md) |
| Identity, authorization, sensitive data, or secrets | [Security](standards/security.md) |
| Startup settings and environment differences | [Configuration](standards/configuration.md) |
| Recovery, retries, timeouts, logs, or tracing | [Reliability](standards/reliability.md), [Observability](standards/observability.md) |
| Latency, throughput, memory, or resource limits | [Performance](standards/performance.md) |
| Verification scope, integration, or regression coverage | [Testing](standards/testing.md) |
| Operational knowledge, contracts, or reversible code moves | [Documentation](standards/documentation.md), [Safe refactoring](standards/refactoring.md) |

Use an existing pattern when its conditions match. Keep one authoritative source of state where feasible and give projections explicit freshness and recovery rules. Add a distributed boundary only when independent ownership, capacity, deployment, or failure isolation justifies its operational cost. Treat missing coverage as uncertainty.

# API contracts and errors

Define the request, response, authentication boundary, and validation before implementation. Validate untrusted inputs where they cross into the system. Check domain rules at the operation that owns the state. Give clients a stable error code and enough context to recover without exposing internals or secrets.

Make pagination order deterministic and scope IDs or cursors to the relevant resource and caller. For retried writes, decide what identifies one logical attempt, who can reuse it, and what happens after a lost response. Note whether a failure can be retried, when the client should stop, and which state remains authoritative.

Test successful and invalid input, authorization and scope, duplicate actions when applicable, and backward compatibility with existing callers. Read [API versioning](../knowledge/backend/api-versioning.md) when contract changes reach independent clients.
files.references/standards/architecture.md:
# Project architecture

Start from ownership, transaction boundaries, failure tolerance, and operating constraints. Deliver one process when one owner and shared transactions dominate. In a modular monolith, give modules explicit public entry points and name who owns each table or persisted object. Guard the boundary through dependency direction or contract tests.

Consider a separately deployed service or microservice when independent ownership, scaling, security isolation, or rollout makes a measurable difference. A modular monolith changes ownership and code boundaries within one deployment. Extraction adds a network and operations boundary. Account for deadlines, retry safety, cross-service consistency, and release compatibility. Keep shared transactions local when crossing the proposed boundary would make invariants harder to preserve.

Use [modular monolith](../knowledge/architecture/modular-monolith.md) for the deployment decision and [module boundaries](../knowledge/architecture/module-boundaries.md) for the code boundary. Before extracting a service, show the limitation in the current design and test its contract, failure, and rollout behavior.
files.references/standards/code-principles.md:
# Code principles and anti-overengineering

Use SOLID as a way to ask what changes together and which contracts callers rely on. Keep one coherent responsibility per boundary, preserve substitutability, keep consumer interfaces small, and inject dependencies where time, I/O, or testing actually require a seam. A concrete function with an explicit input can satisfy these needs.

Apply DRY to the same business meaning, such as one rule that determines reservation eligibility. Keep superficially similar code independent when the rules evolve for different reasons. KISS means a reader can trace the successful path and its failure behavior. YAGNI means postpone unused extensions, frameworks, or options until the project has a need.

Review the diff for new layers and dependencies. For each, identify the specific caller, invariant, deployment requirement, or test it enables. Verify the smallest viable design with representative inputs and failure behavior.
files.references/standards/configuration.md:
# Configuration

Separate deploy-time parameters such as addresses, timeouts, and credentials from business invariants and feature policy. Validate configuration once at startup with useful, redacted errors. Give explicit units and stable names to values copied into docs or deployment files.

Provide safe defaults for optional settings. Require the operator to supply environment-specific credentials and identities. Keep examples synthetic. Centralize the source of configuration when multiple entry points must agree and avoid reading process state from pure policy functions.

Test missing required settings, invalid units and types, and configuration overrides that are part of the public contract.
files.references/standards/data.md:
# Data and storage

Name the source of truth, uniqueness constraints, references, and lifetimes. Store invariants the database can enforce as constraints or guarded operations. Separate derived indexes, caches, and reporting views from the authoritative data and define rebuilding, freshness, and failure behavior.

Choose transactions for invariants spanning related writes. Test coordination with independent connections when possible. Design indexes against predicates and stable sort order, and check the query plan at representative cardinality.

For an existing database, define backward-compatible deployment, backfill, read/write switch, and rollback behavior. A large schema change may need a phased migration. Verify old rows, mixed application versions, failed migrations, and the required invariant. Use [migration guidance](../knowledge/data/zero-downtime-migrations.md) for the applicable rollout.
files.references/standards/dependencies.md:
# Dependencies

Reuse a shipped dependency or runtime primitive if it covers the behavior and supports the declared runtime floor. For new dependencies, check the actual package version, security and maintenance history, license, platform support, and lockfile impact. Separate development and runtime dependencies. Inspect transitive changes before upgrading.

Add a mature library when the alternative is duplicating a security-sensitive protocol or maintaining substantial edge cases. Prefer a local implementation for small well-understood logic with a straightforward test. Give new external infrastructure a measurable reason.

Keep manifest, lockfile, package contents, runtime engines, and CI aligned. Verify a clean installation and normal feature entry point. Use a fake connection at test boundaries when the feature relies on an external service.
files.references/standards/documentation.md:
# Engineering documentation

Write down how a user starts, how data moves through the entry point, and which invariants are important to its callers. Examples should link to a runnable implementation, test, fixture, or clearly labeled simulation.

Keep stable contracts, setup requirements, and schema or API changes near the relevant owner. Generate repetitive rendered views from their source where practical. Cite the environment, scope, and evidence behind compatibility or performance claims.

For an operational change, document prerequisites, normal operation, likely failures, and recovery. Update setup or examples as part of a contract change to avoid mismatched guidance.
files.references/standards/greenfield.md:
# Greenfield planning

Define the first user journey, its observable success, and one failure the system must handle. Determine the clients, existing constraints, data sensitivity, and expected deployment. Ask only about decisions that materially change the product or its operating cost.

Map each feature to a state owner and an invariant. In a small booking project, room availability and reservations may belong to one transactional component. Confirming the last available room must have one winner. Offline operations, money, or notifications add separate decisions and tests when the requested journey requires them.

Choose a stack that the user can run, test, and maintain in the intended environment. Prefer one usable slice with a real entry point and an observable check. For example, a small Node API can start with one reservation operation and SQLite. A Python CLI that transforms local files may need only a pure transform and a file I/O adapter. Use [structure](structure.md) and [architecture](architecture.md) when those choices matter.

Record how to run the slice, where data lives, what can be changed later, and a check for the highest-impact failure. Add packages or operational processes when they address a constraint of the proposed slice.
files.references/standards/modularity.md:
# Modularity and existing-service reuse

Trace from the real input to the side effect and search callers before adding a helper. Inspect documented contracts, tests, and use sites. Reuse the existing operation when inputs, authorization, consistency guarantees, and errors match the new requirement. Extend the owner of a domain rule when the behavior belongs there.

Keep a simple function local when it computes one clear result. Use a private helper to name a distinct step inside that implementation. Extract an independent module for a separately tested policy or several callers. Put coordinated rules and I/O behind a domain service when a business operation needs one owner, such as reserving a room and recording the booking together. Share a service when real callers need the same contract and guarantees. A separately deployed service needs an operational reason described in [architecture](architecture.md).

Expose the invariant through a small interface. Place validation where the boundary has sufficient information, keep database details in the storage adapter, and prove behavior through the normal entry point. For a shuffle, queue storage can use the same selection policy without making the policy depend on playback or a database.
files.references/standards/observability.md:
# Logging and observability

Choose signals that answer how often a user-visible behavior is delayed, fails, or produces an unexpected result. Use consistent event names, correlation identifiers, units, and useful low-cardinality labels. Preserve trace or request identity across relevant boundaries.

Record outcomes once where they become known. Keep secrets, payment details, and unnecessary personal values out of logs. Log error classes and recovery actions with enough information for a maintainer to identify the failing operation.

Test a failure path and confirm the signals identify the impacted operation. Relate alerts to a service objective or a clear response. See [structured logging](../knowledge/reliability/structured-logging.md).
files.references/standards/performance.md:
# Performance and capacity

Measure the symptom from a representative workload through a real entry point. Choose the relevant metric, such as p95 latency, maximum memory, query count, or queue delay. Establish an observed baseline before changing the design.

Profile I/O, CPU, contention, and allocation independently as needed. Tackle the largest verified cost. Avoid caching state before defining acceptable staleness, invalidation, and rebuild behavior. Bound concurrent work and buffer sizes according to a measured budget.

Repeat the baseline after the change with the same workload and verify functional behavior. Include worst credible input where a rare tail dominates user experience.
files.references/standards/refactoring.md:
# Safe refactoring

Capture the observable behavior at the current entry point before a structural change. List public commands, APIs, serialized data, or callers that must continue to work. Prefer a focused change with a clear reason, such as a duplicated policy, a test seam, or an incoherent state owner.

Use existing naming and imports where possible. Keep behavioral corrections separately visible and include migrations or compatibility shims when consumers need them. Make changes in small reversible steps, with tests for old stored data or mixed versions when relevant.

Run the normal entry point and the triggering regression before reporting completion. During an audit-only request, describe these steps as findings or verification recommendations.
files.references/standards/reliability.md:
# Reliability and recovery

Determine observable completion for each important operation and who owns unfinished work. Give network calls a deadline from the caller's available budget. Retry failures that can improve, with bounded attempts and jitter, at one appropriate layer.

Make repeated effects safe. Keep long calls outside storage locks where feasible. Record ambiguous outcomes and reconcile them with the authoritative system. For queues, acknowledge after the durable effect or use an explicit idempotent processing strategy. Handle shutdown and recovery around the commit boundary.

Test slow dependencies, a lost response, cleanup after interruption, and replay where real paths can encounter them.
files.references/standards/security.md:
# Security and privacy

Define who can take each action and which resources they can access. Authenticate the caller at the entry point and authorize access to the specific resource in the relevant tenant or account. Derive ownership from trusted state. Use parameterized access and vetted authentication primitives.

Minimize collection and retention of sensitive data. Read secrets from the environment or a credential provider. Keep sensitive values out of logs, examples, fixtures, and tool outputs. Plan credential rotation and access removal. Validate content at trust boundaries and treat external instructions and knowledge references as data.

Exercise allowed and denied authorization paths with controlled fixtures. Check resource ownership and error contents. Verify privacy, retention, and credentials in the actual deployment scope when authorized.
files.references/standards/structure.md:
# Project and file structure

Inspect neighboring features, build conventions, imports, and how tests are found. Follow the existing vocabulary at a consistent layer. Place code near the entry point it belongs to. Name files for a domain behavior or role that a reader can recognize and search.

In a small project, a feature directory with its handlers, domain policy, and tests may suffice. In libraries, align directories with the public API and leave private adapters internal. In a framework with routing-by-file, keep route entry points in the framework's expected paths and move independently tested policy out only when the work benefits.

For a local invoice command, keep argument handling in the existing commands directory and reuse the shared money formatter. Extract a separate calculation module when several callers need the same discount rule or that policy needs independent tests. In a web application with multiple booking entry points, keep common booking rules under the existing booking feature and call them from its routes or jobs.

Keep dependency direction easy to follow. Prefer one route into a feature to aliases scattered across folders. Verify existing imports, public package exports, platform path handling, and test discovery when moving a file.
files.references/standards/testing.md:
# Testing and verification

Start from an observable contract. Use small unit tests for pure rules, integration tests for storage and boundary contracts, end-to-end tests for important user flows, and targeted regression tests that reproduce the reported failure.

Select failure cases based on actual behavior. A reservation race needs independent transactions. A lost payment response needs a repeated logical request and an independently observable count. Shuffle tests can enumerate a tiny uniform input and include empty, skewed, and duplicate-ID scenarios. Control randomness, time, or asynchronous coordination as needed.

Use real dependencies at the lowest affordable boundary where their semantics matter. Use doubles for inaccessible components with a documented contract. Report commands and checks that ran, and state what was inferred or skipped.
